title: Beetroot Cutlet Recipe: How To Make Crispy Tikki at Home
excerpt: This vibrant beetroot tikki combines grated beets, mashed potato, and Indian spices into a crispy, protein-rich snack that works as an evening nibble, party starter, or even a burger patty.
body:
• Beetroot cutlets require just grated beetroot, one boiled potato, breadcrumbs, and a handful of Indian spices — total prep-to-plate time is about 30 minutes.
  • The tikki can be deep-fried, shallow-fried, air-fried, or baked at 180°C for 25 minutes, making it adaptable to any kitchen setup or health preference.
  • Beetroot is rich in dietary nitrates, folate, iron, and betalain antioxidants, according to research published in Food Science & Nutrition and reviewed by Medanta.
  • The cutlets double as burger patties, sandwich fillings, or wrap stuffing — a versatile base for weeknight meals.

The Humble Tikki With a Health Halo

Among India's vast repertoire of teatime snacks, the beetroot cutlet occupies a quiet but devoted corner. Unlike its flashier cousins — the aloo tikki of chaat carts or the bread-crumbed mutton cutlet of Kolkata roll shops — the beetroot version wins fans with a vivid magenta colour that requires zero artificial dye and a nutritional profile that few fried snacks can match.

The recipe has circulated in South Indian homes and restaurant menus for decades. According to Hebbar's Kitchen, one of India's most-followed food platforms with 188 five-star ratings on this recipe alone, the beetroot cutlet draws particular fame from Karnataka's restaurant culture, where establishments like the well-known Diana Restaurant in Mangalore serve it coated in roasted rava for an extra-crisp shell.

Ingredients You Will Need

The cutlet mixture is straightforward. For roughly six servings, according to Hebbar's Kitchen:

For the patties: 2 cups grated beetroot (juice squeezed out), 1 boiled and mashed potato, ¼ finely chopped onion, ¼ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri red chilli powder, ¼ tsp cumin powder, ½ tsp garam masala, ½ tsp amchur (dry mango powder), ½ tsp chaat masala, ½ tsp ginger-garlic paste, ¼ cup breadcrumbs, 2 tbsp chopped coriander, and salt to taste.

For the coating: 2 tbsp corn flour, 1 tbsp plain flour, ½ tsp crushed pepper, ¼ tsp salt, and ¼ cup water — whisked into a smooth batter. Plus 1 cup breadcrumbs for the outer layer and oil for frying.

Step-by-Step Method

Start by squeezing out excess juice from the grated beetroot — this single step determines whether the cutlets hold together or fall apart. Transfer the pressed beetroot to a mixing bowl, add the mashed potato, onion, all the spice powders, breadcrumbs, and coriander. Combine until a firm dough forms.

Shape the mixture into round, flat patties roughly 6–7 cm across. Prepare the corn flour batter in a separate bowl. Dip each patty into the batter, then roll in breadcrumbs until evenly coated on both sides.

For shallow frying, heat a flat pan with 2–3 teaspoons of oil and cook on medium flame until golden on each side — roughly 3–4 minutes per side, according to Cooking From Heart. Deep-frying in hot oil takes about the same time. For a healthier route, bake at 180°C for 25 minutes, flipping once, or air-fry at the same temperature until crisp.

Drain on kitchen paper and serve immediately with green chutney, tomato ketchup, or a mint-yoghurt dip.

Variations Worth Trying

Tarla Dalal's version swaps the potato for grated carrot and a soaked bread slice, creating a lighter tikki with a slightly sweeter flavour. Archana's Kitchen adds chickpeas and crushed peanuts for extra protein, while Being Rubitah uses leftover rajma curry as a binder — an ingenious zero-waste twist that also makes the cutlet vegan and gluten-free when semolina replaces breadcrumbs.

Chef Ashok's stuffed version folds paneer into the centre and coats the cutlet with breadcrumbs for a richer party appetiser.

Why Beetroot Deserves a Place on Your Plate

Beyond colour and taste, beetroot brings serious nutritional weight. A half-cup serving contains just 37 calories, according to Medanta. The root is rich in dietary nitrates that the body converts into nitric oxide, which relaxes blood vessels and helps lower blood pressure. Research published in the journal Food Science & Nutrition found that betalains — the pigments behind beetroot's red hue — act as antioxidants that reduce oxidative stress and may inhibit cell damage.

Beets also supply folate for cell growth, iron in quantities that exceed spinach gram-for-gram according to Northwestern Medicine, and fibre that supports gut health and blood-sugar regulation. For athletes, nitrate-rich beetroot has been shown to improve exercise efficiency and endurance.

A Diaspora Kitchen Staple

For Indian families abroad, the beetroot cutlet is one of the easiest street-food classics to replicate. Beetroot, potatoes, and standard spice-rack staples like garam masala and chaat masala are widely available in mainstream supermarkets across North America, Europe, and the Middle East — no trip to a specialty Indian grocery required. The cutlets freeze well before the coating stage, making them a practical make-ahead snack for weeknight dinners or potluck gatherings.

They also slide neatly into fusion territory: use them as a burger patty with a brioche bun, tuck them into a wrap with hummus, or crumble them over a salad for a warm, spiced topping.

Tips for the Best Results

Squeeze the grated beetroot thoroughly — excess moisture is the number-one reason cutlets fall apart during frying. If the mixture still feels wet, add an extra tablespoon of breadcrumbs or cornstarch. Refrigerating shaped patties for 15–20 minutes before coating firms them up further. And resist the urge to crowd the pan: frying in batches of two or three ensures even browning and a crisp crust all around.
nri_angle: Beetroot cutlets are a simple way for diaspora cooks to recreate a beloved Indian street snack with ingredients available at any grocery store abroad.
